chunks: Intercalating a month is adding to unbelief. The unbelievers are misguided by this, for they take the same month to be sacred one year and sacrilegious the next, thus making the number of months sanctified by God accord with theirs in order to make what God has forbidden, lawful. Attractive seem to them their evil deeds; but God does not show the unbelievers the way.

key_terms.النَّسِي‌ءُ: Intercalation; the practice of adding or subtracting months from the lunar calendar
key_terms.الکُفْرِ: Unbelief; specifically the disbelief associated with distorting divine law
key_terms.سُوءُ أَعْمَالِهِمْ: The evil of their deeds; the ugliness or attractiveness of their bad actions as perceived by themselves
key_terms.لِيُوَاطِئُوا: So that they may make equal; referring to the intent to match the number of sacred months with their own count
key_terms.يُحَرِّمُونَهُ: They make it sacrilegious/forbidden; referring to the act of declaring permissible months as sacred
key_terms.يُحِلُّونَهُ: They make it lawful; referring to the act of declaring sacred months as permissible for war or other activities

ai.seo_question: What is Nasi and how did the pre-Islamic Arabs use it to alter divine law?
ai.summary: In Shia exegesis, this verse is often linked to the specific practice of the Quraysh, who added a thirteenth month to synchronize the lunar calendar with the solar agricultural cycle, thereby manipulating the sanctity of the four sacred months. This 'intercalation' (Nasi') served as a mechanism to legitimize their own actions by declaring previously forbidden months lawful, illustrating how superficial adherence to divine law can mask deeper unbelief (Kufr). The verse underscores that God does not guide those who distort His commands to suit their desires, a principle that extends to the preservation of the lunar calendar's integrity in Islamic jurisprudence.
